subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Escape Velocity and Gravity
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Escape Velocity and Gravity.

hook.text: Every object has an escape velocity—the speed needed to break free of its gravity. Earth's is 11.2 km/s.

buildup.text: The more massive and compact an object, the higher its escape velocity. Neutron stars need 100,000 km/s.

discovery.text: A black hole's escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Since nothing travels faster, nothing escapes.

twist.text: This means a black hole doesn't suck things in. It traps things that get too close—like a cosmic pitfall.

climax.text: If the Sun became a black hole, Earth wouldn't be sucked in. It would keep orbiting—just in total darkness.

punchline.text: Not a vacuum cleaner. A trap for anything that crosses the line.

quiz.question: What would happen to Earth's orbit if the Sun became a black hole of the same mass?
options: Earth would continue orbiting normally since the gravitational pull stays the same
Earth would be sucked into the black hole immediately
Earth would fly off into space without the Sun's light

details.summary: Escape velocity is the speed needed to break free from an object's gravitational pull. Earth's is 11.2 km/s; the Sun's is 618 km/s. A black hole's escape velocity at the event horizon exceeds the speed of light — which is why nothing, not even light, can escape.
details.whyItMatters: Escape velocity connects everyday gravity to black hole physics. Understanding this single concept explains why black holes are black and why the speed of light sets the ultimate boundary.
takeaways: Escape velocity is the speed needed to overcome gravity
At a black hole's event horizon it exceeds light speed
This is why nothing can escape a black hole

faq.question: Does a black hole pull harder than a star of equal mass?
faq.answer: No — at the same distance, gravity is identical. The difference is compactness. A black hole's mass is concentrated so tightly that you can get close enough for escape velocity to exceed light speed. A star's surface keeps you far from its center.

faq.question: Could a spaceship ever escape a black hole?
faq.answer: Not from inside the event horizon — that would require faster-than-light travel, which violates relativity. Outside the horizon, escape is possible with sufficient thrust. The closer you orbit, the more energy escape requires, but it remains theoretically possible.
